items.title: The halting problem
items.claim: Alan Turing's 1936 paper proved a famous result about algorithms. What did it show?

options.text: No general algorithm can determine in advance whether an arbitrary program halts

items.reveal:
Turing's 1936 paper 'On Computable Numbers' established that no algorithm can correctly answer 'does program P halt on input I?' for all P, I.

The proof uses a diagonal argument similar to Cantor's.
items.why: Computing has provable limits, set out before the first electronic computer was built.

items.title: P versus NP
items.claim: The P vs NP question is the most famous open problem in computer science. Which statement describes its current status?

options.text: It has been proven that P equals NP
It has been proven that P does not equal NP
It is one of the Clay Millennium Prize problems and remains open

items.reveal_title: Open since 1971 and worth a million dollars
items.reveal:
Stephen Cook (1971) and Leonid Levin (1973) independently formalised the question. The Clay Mathematics Institute offers one of seven Millennium Prizes for its resolution.

Most researchers conjecture P does not equal NP, but no proof exists.
items.why: If P=NP, problems whose solutions can be checked quickly could also be found quickly — including breaking most modern encryption.

items.title: Moore's Law slowing
items.claim: Gordon Moore's 1965 observation predicted transistor counts roughly doubling every 18-24 months. What is its current status?

options.text: It continues at the original pace
Doubling has slowed; per-transistor cost reductions have largely stalled

items.reveal:
Industry analyses since the mid-2010s show progress shifting from feature shrink to architectural changes, chiplets and specialised accelerators.

Jensen Huang and others have publicly described Moore's Law as effectively over in its original form.
items.why: Architectural innovation now does more of the work than raw process scaling once did.

items.title: What RSA depends on
items.claim: RSA encryption (Rivest, Shamir, Adleman, 1977) relies on the practical difficulty of which mathematical operation?

options.text: Factoring the product of two large primes

items.reveal:
RSA's security rests on the gap between multiplying two large primes (easy) and recovering them from the product (currently hard for sufficient bit lengths).

Shor's 1994 algorithm shows a sufficiently large quantum computer would break RSA.
items.why: Modern cryptography is a bet that certain mathematical problems remain hard. Quantum computing threatens that bet.

items.title: ARPANET's first message
items.claim: On 29 October 1969 the first ARPANET message was sent between UCLA and SRI (Stanford Research Institute). What did the operator manage to transmit before the system crashed?
items.reveal:
Charley Kline at UCLA typed 'L' and 'O' before the system at Stanford failed. The connection was restored about an hour later and the full LOGIN went through.

ARPANET grew to four nodes by December 1969.
items.why: Even foundational milestones often begin with mundane failures rather than dramatic success.

items.title: Why Berners-Lee built the web
items.claim: Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989. What was the immediate motivation?
items.reveal:
Berners-Lee's March 1989 proposal 'Information Management: A Proposal' addressed the problem of staff turnover and lost documentation in a large physics organisation.

CERN released the underlying code into the public domain in 1993.
items.why: Releasing the protocol openly was a choice that shaped the web's evolution.

items.title: The first computer 'bug'
items.claim: In 1947 a literal insect was taped into a log book at Harvard. Who was the engineer most associated with the incident?
items.reveal_title: Grace Hopper's team at Harvard Mark II
items.reveal:
A moth was found jamming a relay in the Mark II computer on 9 September 1947 and taped into the log with the note 'First actual case of bug being found'.

The term 'bug' had been used in engineering since at least Edison.
items.why: Terminology often predates its famous origin story; jargon collects illustrative anecdotes.

items.title: Comparison sort lower bound
items.claim: Any comparison-based sorting algorithm has a proven lower bound on its worst-case time complexity. What is it?
items.reveal:
The proof uses the decision-tree model: a comparison-based sort must distinguish between n! permutations, requiring at least log2(n!) comparisons, which is theta(n log n).

Non-comparison sorts (radix, counting) can be faster on restricted inputs.
items.why: Lower bounds tell you when further algorithmic optimisation is impossible without changing model assumptions.

items.title: GPL and copyleft
items.claim: Richard Stallman launched the GNU project in 1983 and wrote the GPL licence. What property defines 'copyleft'?

options.text: Software must be free of charge
Derivative works must also be distributed under the same licence
Only the original author may modify it

items.reveal:
Copyleft uses copyright law to ensure freedoms are preserved downstream. GPL v2 (1991) and v3 (2007) are the most widely deployed copyleft licences.

Permissive licences (MIT, BSD, Apache) take a different approach by not requiring share-alike.
items.why: Software freedom is a legal architecture, not just a technical one.

items.title: 0.1 + 0.2 in IEEE 754
items.claim: In most programming languages using IEEE 754 double-precision arithmetic, what does 0.1 + 0.2 evaluate to?
items.reveal:
Neither 0.1 nor 0.2 has an exact binary representation. The standard IEEE 754 double evaluates the sum to 0.30000000000000004.

Decimal or arbitrary-precision libraries are used where this matters (finance, audit).
items.why: Numerical errors emerge from representation, not arithmetic mistakes.

items.title: The birthday paradox
items.claim: In a group of 23 people, what is the approximate probability that at least two share a birthday?
items.reveal:
The probability passes 50% at 23 people and 99% at 70. The result drives the 'birthday attack' on hash functions: finding a collision needs roughly 2^(n/2) trials, not 2^n.

This is why hash outputs are commonly 256 bits.
items.why: Intuition about probability is unreliable, and cryptographic design must account for it.

items.title: When SHA-1 broke
items.claim: In 2017 Google and CWI announced 'SHAttered', the first practical collision in SHA-1. About how much computation did it take?
items.reveal_title: Thousands of CPU-years to break SHA-1
items.reveal:
The 2017 SHAttered attack required roughly 6,500 CPU-years of computation. By 2020 the SHA-1 chosen-prefix attack (Leurent and Peyrin) cost about $45,000 on rented GPUs.

SHA-1 is now deprecated in major standards.
items.why: Cryptographic 'breaks' become economic problems before they become practical attacks.

items.title: Latency differences
items.claim: L1 cache access takes about 1 ns. Roughly how long does a fetch from main memory take by comparison?
items.reveal:
Approximate figures (Jeff Dean's 'numbers everyone should know'): L1 cache 1 ns, main memory 100 ns, SSD 100 microseconds, disk seek 10 ms.

The ratios drive cache-friendly algorithm design.
items.why: Algorithm choice often matters less than memory layout once data exceeds cache size.

items.title: The ELIZA effect
items.claim: Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA chatbot (1966) used simple keyword matching. What was Weizenbaum's reaction when his secretary engaged emotionally with it?

options.text: He was thrilled and commercialised it
He became a sharp critic of attributing understanding to machines

items.reveal_title: ELIZA's creator turned into one of AI's earliest critics
items.reveal:
Weizenbaum's 1976 book Computer Power and Human Reason argued against using computers in roles requiring human judgement.

The 'ELIZA effect' describes the human tendency to attribute understanding to systems that have none.
items.why: Creators often see clearly what users want to project. The pattern recurs with each new generation of chatbots.

items.title: First normal form forbids repeating groups
items.claim: A 'customers' table has columns customer_id, name and phone_numbers where phone_numbers contains comma-separated values like '0207...,0790...'. Which normal form is violated?

options.text: First normal form — atomicity is violated; each cell must hold a single, indivisible value

items.reveal:
Codd's 1970 paper 'A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks' introduced normalisation. 1NF requires atomic values; 2NF removes partial dependencies on a composite key; 3NF removes transitive dependencies.

The fix here is a separate phone_numbers table with foreign key customer_id, supporting one-to-many. The comma-separated workaround breaks indexing, queries (LIKE searches instead of joins) and integrity constraints.
items.why: Schemas that violate 1NF look convenient until queries get complex. Most real-world database performance problems trace back to design decisions like this.

items.title: ACID is four properties, not one
items.claim: ACID is the standard guarantee for relational database transactions. What does the 'I' stand for and what does it guarantee?

options.text: Indexing — every column must be indexed
Isolation — concurrent transactions appear to execute as if they were serial; intermediate states aren't visible to other transactions
Idempotency — repeated execution gives same result

items.reveal:
Coined by Andreas Reuter and Theo Härder in 1983. Atomicity: all-or-nothing. Consistency: invariants hold before and after. Isolation: concurrent transactions don't interfere. Durability: committed changes survive crashes.

Isolation levels are tunable (read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read, serializable) — stronger isolation costs throughput. Most production databases default to read committed, not full serializable.
items.why: ACID makes correctness easier to reason about. Distributed systems often relax these guarantees (BASE) for availability — a different trade-off.

items.title: SQL injection still tops the OWASP charts
items.claim: A login form constructs the query "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '" + input + "'". What happens if a user enters: admin' OR '1'='1

options.text: The query rejects the malformed input
The WHERE clause becomes always-true, returning all users and likely logging the attacker in as the first one (often admin)

items.reveal:
The constructed query becomes: SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = 'admin' OR '1'='1'. Since '1'='1' is always true, all rows return. Parameterised queries (prepared statements) prevent this by separating SQL code from data.

The 2017 Equifax breach (143 million records) exploited an Apache Struts vulnerability; SQL injection has been in OWASP Top 10 since 2003 and remains there. The 2008 Heartland Payment Systems breach (130m cards) also began with SQL injection.
items.why: A class of attack with a known fix (parameterised queries) keeps appearing because developers concatenate strings. Defensive coding patterns must be the default, not the exception.

items.title: NoSQL trades joins for scale
items.claim: MongoDB stores data as JSON-like documents. Compared to a relational database, what's the main trade-off?

options.text: Document stores are always faster for any query type
Flexible schema and horizontal scaling come at the cost of weaker ACID guarantees and harder cross-document joins; suits hierarchical data, struggles with highly relational data

items.reveal:
Eric Brewer's CAP theorem (2000) formalised the trade-off: a distributed system can guarantee at most two of Consistency, Availability and Partition tolerance. NoSQL systems (Cassandra, DynamoDB, MongoDB) typically chose AP, sacrificing strong consistency for availability under partition.

By the late 2010s the picture had blurred: PostgreSQL added JSONB support, MongoDB added multi-document transactions (4.0, 2018). 'NoSQL vs SQL' became 'choose the right store for your access patterns'.
items.why: Database choice is about query patterns and consistency requirements, not which is 'modern'. Both relational and document stores have grown to overlap considerably.

items.title: Indexes speed reads but cost writes and space
items.claim: A 10-million-row users table has an index on the email column. What is the main trade-off compared to no index?

options.text: Lookups by email go from O(n) to O(log n), but every insert/update/delete must also update the index, and the index consumes additional disk space (often 1-3% of table size per index)

items.reveal:
Most relational databases use B-tree indexes (typically B+ trees). Sequential reads through 10m rows take seconds; an index lookup takes microseconds.

Write-heavy tables can become slower with too many indexes — every INSERT updates each index. The art of database tuning is choosing which indexes to create and which queries to support; index every column and writes slow to a crawl. PostgreSQL also offers GIN, GiST, BRIN and hash indexes for specific query patterns.
items.why: There is no free performance. Every index has a cost in writes and storage. Profiling matters more than instinct.

items.title: The OSI model has 7 layers; the internet uses 4-5
items.claim: The OSI reference model defines 7 layers. The actual internet protocol stack (TCP/IP) is usually described in how many?

options.text: 4 or 5 (link, internet, transport, application — sometimes physical split out) — OSI is a teaching model; TCP/IP is what runs

items.reveal_title: OSI is taught, TCP/IP is used
items.reveal:
ISO/OSI was finalised in 1984. By then, TCP/IP (from 1974) had already been adopted by ARPANET (1983) and was on its way to becoming the de facto internet stack.

OSI's session and presentation layers map onto TCP/IP's application layer. The reference model survives as a teaching tool and a layer-numbering convention ('Layer 7 load balancer', 'Layer 2 switch') but few production systems implement OSI directly.
items.why: Standards bodies design clean abstractions; production systems use whatever works. The gap between OSI and TCP/IP is a small case study in that pattern.

items.title: HTTPS encrypts content but leaks metadata
items.claim: When you visit https://example.com/private-page, what does an observer on the network see?

options.text: The destination IP and the SNI (typically the hostname example.com) are visible; the path /private-page, headers and body are encrypted by TLS
The full URL and content in plain text
Only the IP address — even the hostname is hidden

items.reveal:
TLS (the protocol behind the 'S' in HTTPS) encrypts the HTTP request and response. But the TLS handshake itself currently sends the Server Name Indication (SNI) in clear so that one IP can host many sites. Encrypted Client Hello (ECH), standardised 2024, is rolling out to fix this.

DNS lookups are also typically unencrypted unless DNS-over-HTTPS or DNS-over-TLS is in use. Browser HTTPS protects content well; broader network anonymity needs additional tools.
items.why: Encryption is not equivalent to privacy. Metadata (who you talk to, when, how often) often reveals more than content.

items.title: DNS is hierarchical and cached at every layer
items.claim: When your browser resolves www.example.com, what's the typical path?

options.text: Browser cache → OS cache → recursive resolver (often ISP) → root servers (.) → TLD servers (.com) → authoritative server for example.com — with caching at each layer based on TTL
Sends an email to a registrar

items.reveal:
Paul Mockapetris designed DNS in 1983 (RFC 882/883), replacing a single HOSTS.TXT file maintained at Stanford. There are 13 root server identifiers (A-M), each implemented as anycast clusters of hundreds of physical servers worldwide.

The 2016 Mirai botnet attack on Dyn (a major DNS provider) showed how DNS centralisation creates single points of failure — Twitter, Spotify, Reddit and others were intermittently unreachable.
items.why: DNS is the invisible glue of the web. Its caching makes the system fast; its centralisation is a security concern; its hierarchy ties human-readable names to numerical addresses.

items.title: You can't beat the speed of light
items.claim: Light travels through fibre optic at about 200,000 km/s. What's the minimum theoretical round-trip latency from London to Sydney (~17,000 km direct)?

options.text: Around 170 ms minimum (2 x 17,000 / 200,000 seconds), without including routing or processing delays; real values run 250-300 ms

items.reveal:
Light in fibre travels at roughly 2/3 c (slowed by the refractive index of glass). Stuart Cheshire's 1996 essay 'It's the Latency, Stupid' pointed out that bandwidth can be improved by adding capacity; latency is bounded by physics.

This is why content delivery networks (CDNs) cache content geographically near users, and why high-frequency trading firms colocate servers in exchange data centres.
items.why: Bandwidth and latency are independent. Doubling your line speed doesn't reduce ping times. This shapes architectural decisions for any global service.

items.title: BGP runs the internet on trust
items.claim: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is how internet networks decide routes between each other. What is its main security weakness?

options.text: BGP is fully secured by default
Historically, BGP accepted any 'route announcement' from connected networks without cryptographic verification; misconfiguration or malice can hijack traffic globally within minutes
BGP only works inside data centres

items.reveal:
BGP was standardised in 1989 (RFC 1105). It assumes participating networks announce only routes they actually serve. Famous incidents: Pakistan Telecom's 2008 attempt to block YouTube nationally inadvertently routed YouTube traffic globally into a black hole for 2 hours; the 2021 Facebook outage was triggered by a BGP misconfiguration that withdrew Facebook's routes worldwide.

RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) is being rolled out to cryptographically authenticate route origins, but adoption is partial.
items.why: The internet's most foundational routing protocol assumes goodwill among operators. The system works astonishingly well most of the time and fails spectacularly when it doesn't.

items.title: Stateful firewalls track connections, not just packets
items.claim: A stateful firewall differs from a stateless packet filter how?

options.text: Stateful firewalls remember active connections; replies on established TCP sessions are allowed without re-evaluation against rules. Stateless filters evaluate each packet independently

items.reveal:
Cisco PIX (1994) was an early commercial stateful firewall. Tracking connection state allows simpler rules: 'allow outbound, allow replies to outbound' instead of complex bidirectional packet rules.

Deep packet inspection (DPI) firewalls go further, examining application-layer content. Next-generation firewalls (NGFW) combine stateful filtering with intrusion prevention, application identification and TLS inspection. Cloud-native firewalls (security groups, NSGs) typically operate at L4 statefully.
items.why: The shift from packet to connection awareness made firewalls usable in practice. Modern systems extend this to application awareness.

items.title: IPv4 addresses ran out — but slowly
items.claim: IPv4 provides ~4.3 billion (2^32) addresses. When did the IANA assign its last free /8 block?

options.text: 2011 — IANA exhausted the central pool on 3 February 2011; the regional registries (APNIC, RIPE, ARIN, LACNIC, AFRINIC) ran out over the following years

items.reveal:
IPv6 (2^128 addresses) was standardised in 1998 (RFC 2460) in anticipation. Despite this, IPv6 adoption took two decades — by 2024 Google measured around 45% of users reaching it over IPv6.

IPv4 stayed usable through NAT (Network Address Translation), allowing many devices to share one public address, and through markets in IPv4 blocks (a /16 traded for around $1m by 2023).
items.why: Standards adoption is shaped by economics, not just technology. NAT extended IPv4's lifetime by decades — at the cost of breaking the end-to-end principle the internet was originally designed around.

items.title: In public-key crypto, you publish one key and keep the other secret
items.claim: Alice wants to send Bob an encrypted message using RSA. Whose key does she use to encrypt?

options.text: Bob's public key — only Bob's private key can decrypt the result, so anyone can send Bob secret messages but only Bob can read them
A shared secret she and Bob agreed in person

items.reveal_title: Encrypt with public, decrypt with private
items.reveal:
Digital signatures invert the operation: Alice signs with her private key; anyone can verify with her public key. Combined, these enable both confidentiality and authentication on open networks.

Diffie and Hellman's 1976 paper 'New Directions in Cryptography' introduced the concept. RSA (1977) was the first widely deployed implementation. Elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC) offers similar security at smaller key sizes — important for low-power devices.
items.why: The asymmetric model lets strangers establish secure channels. Before it, every pair of communicators needed to pre-share a secret somehow.

items.title: Hashing is one-way; encryption is reversible
items.claim: A password manager stores user passwords. Which approach is appropriate?

options.text: Store a salted hash (using bcrypt, scrypt or argon2) — passwords cannot be recovered from the hash, only verified by re-hashing user input. Encryption would be wrong here because no system needs to recover the plaintext
Encrypt with the user's password as the key

items.reveal_title: Hash for verification, encrypt for transmission
items.reveal:
Common confusion: hashing is one-way (no key, no recovery); encryption is two-way (with a key, recoverable). For password storage, you only need to verify; hashing fits.

Password-specific hash functions (bcrypt 1999, scrypt 2009, Argon2 2015 — the Password Hashing Competition winner) are deliberately slow and memory-hard to resist brute-force attacks. The 2012 LinkedIn breach exposed 6.5m unsalted SHA-1 password hashes; a third were cracked within days.
items.why: Choosing the right cryptographic primitive matters more than choosing a strong one. SHA-256 is strong; using it for passwords (without proper KDF) is still wrong.

items.title: Ransomware uses cryptography for harm
items.claim: The WannaCry ransomware (May 2017) hit hundreds of thousands of computers including the UK NHS. What enabled its rapid spread?

options.text: EternalBlue — an SMB protocol exploit leaked from the NSA — let WannaCry propagate worm-like without user action across unpatched Windows systems

items.reveal:
EternalBlue was developed by the NSA and stolen by the Shadow Brokers group, who released it in April 2017. Microsoft had patched the underlying vulnerability (MS17-010) two months earlier; many systems were unpatched.

WannaCry hit at least 200,000 systems in 150 countries. The NHS in England estimated direct costs of £92m and cancelled around 19,000 appointments. The kill switch was found accidentally by security researcher Marcus Hutchins.
items.why: Cyber risks aren't only criminal. State-developed offensive capabilities leak. The defensive value of patch hygiene is hard to overstate.

items.title: ML systems inherit and amplify training bias
items.claim: ProPublica's 2016 analysis of the COMPAS risk-assessment algorithm used in US courts found what pattern?

options.text: COMPAS had identical error rates across racial groups
Black defendants were nearly twice as likely as white defendants to be falsely flagged as high risk; white defendants were more often falsely flagged as low risk
The algorithm was perfectly fair by all metrics

items.reveal:
Julia Angwin's ProPublica team analysed 7,000 COMPAS scores in Broward County, Florida. They found unequal false-positive and false-negative rates by race.

Northpointe (now Equivant) responded that COMPAS satisfied a different fairness criterion (predictive parity). Chouldechova's 2017 paper showed mathematically that with unequal base rates, you cannot satisfy all three common fairness criteria simultaneously — the trade-off is irreducible.

The ethical question isn't just technical: which fairness criterion you choose embeds a value judgment.
items.why: ML 'fairness' is not a single property and may not be achievable on all metrics simultaneously. Engineering choices encode social decisions.

items.title: Snowden disclosures revealed bulk metadata collection
items.claim: Edward Snowden's 2013 disclosures revealed extensive intelligence programmes. Which is most accurate about PRISM?

options.text: PRISM was a programme for monitoring weather data
PRISM was a US National Security Agency programme collecting communications data from major US tech firms (Google, Microsoft, Yahoo, Facebook, Apple and others) under FISA Section 702

items.reveal:
The Guardian and Washington Post published Snowden's disclosures from June 2013. They revealed PRISM, XKeyscore, Tempora (GCHQ) and Bullrun (NSA's programme to weaken commercial encryption).

The disclosures drove industry-wide adoption of stronger encryption defaults (HTTPS-by-default, end-to-end encrypted messaging) and legal changes (USA Freedom Act 2015 ended bulk telephony metadata collection). The European Court of Justice's Schrems II ruling (2020) invalidated EU-US data transfer arrangements partly citing US surveillance.

Snowden remains in Russia, granted citizenship 2022.
items.why: The architecture of communications systems shapes what surveillance is possible. End-to-end encryption design was reshaped by the disclosures.

items.title: GDPR fines scale to global turnover
items.claim: The EU General Data Protection Regulation came into force in May 2018. What's the maximum fine structure?

options.text: Up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher, for the most serious breaches
There are no fines, only warnings

items.reveal:
GDPR's Article 83 sets two tiers: up to €10m or 2% turnover for record-keeping/notification breaches; €20m or 4% turnover for breaches of basic principles or rights. Largest fines: Meta €1.2bn (2023, EU-US data transfers); Amazon €746m (2021, Luxembourg); Google €90m (CNIL, 2021).

UK GDPR (post-Brexit) mirrors the structure. ICO's Information Commissioner's Office is the UK enforcement body.
items.why: Linking penalties to global turnover ensures consequences are meaningful for multinationals. Pre-GDPR fines were too small to influence behaviour.

items.title: Bug bounties pay for finding flaws
items.claim: Google's Vulnerability Reward Program pays security researchers for discovering and responsibly disclosing flaws. What scale has this reached by 2023?

options.text: Google does not pay for vulnerability disclosure
Google has paid out over $59 million in bounties since 2010, with individual top awards exceeding $1 million for full-chain exploits

items.reveal:
Google launched the VRP in 2010. The model spread: Microsoft, Apple, Meta, the US Department of Defense (Hack the Pentagon, 2016) all run bug bounty programmes. HackerOne and Bugcrowd are platforms that mediate between researchers and firms.

The alternative to bounties is the grey market (Zerodium, NSO Group), where exploits sell to governments and brokers — and end up in offensive tools. Bounty programmes try to make ethical disclosure economically competitive.
items.why: Markets shape behaviour. If finding flaws is more profitable to sell than to disclose, expect more sale than disclosure. Bounty programmes are an attempt to tilt that balance.

items.title: Big-O describes worst-case growth, not actual runtime
items.claim: Algorithm A runs in O(n) time; algorithm B runs in O(log n) time. For very small n, which is always faster?

options.text: Big-O hides constant factors and lower-order terms; for small n, an O(n) algorithm with small constants can outperform an O(log n) algorithm with large ones — sort routines often switch to insertion sort below ~32 elements for this reason

items.reveal:
Donald Knuth popularised Big-O notation for algorithm analysis in his 'Art of Computer Programming' (1968 onwards). It captures asymptotic growth — what happens as n gets large.

Real implementations matter: Timsort (used in Python, Java) is O(n log n) but uses insertion sort for small runs because cache-friendly linear passes beat divide-and-conquer overhead. SIMD vectorisation, cache layout and branch prediction can dominate Big-O differences in practice.
items.why: Asymptotic analysis identifies which algorithm scales. Picking the right one for production needs profiling on representative data.

items.title: Quicksort is usually fast but has a worst case
items.claim: Quicksort and Mergesort are both O(n log n) on average. Where do they differ?

options.text: Quicksort is O(n^2) in worst case (e.g. already-sorted input with naive pivot choice) but in-place and cache-friendly. Mergesort guarantees O(n log n) but needs O(n) extra memory
Quicksort needs more memory than Mergesort

items.reveal:
Tony Hoare invented Quicksort in 1959 while at Moscow State University. With random or median-of-three pivot, the expected runtime is O(n log n) and the in-place property makes it the standard library sort in C (qsort), Java (for primitives) and many others.

Introsort (Musser, 1997) mitigates the worst case by falling back to Heapsort when recursion depth exceeds a threshold. Timsort (Python 2002, Java 2009) is a hybrid Mergesort optimised for partially-sorted real-world data.
items.why: Algorithm choice depends on inputs and constraints. Worst case matters for adversarial inputs (security); average case for benign ones.

items.title: Binary search needs sorted data
items.claim: Binary search runs in O(log n) on a sorted array. For an unsorted array of 1 million items searched once, which is faster?

options.text: Linear search — sorting first takes O(n log n), much more than a single O(n) linear pass. Sorting pays off only when many searches will be performed on the same data

items.reveal:
If you'll search k times, total cost: linear search k*n; binary search n log n + k log n. Binary wins when k > log n / (1 - log n / n), roughly when k exceeds ~20 for n = 1m.

Jon Bentley wrote in 1986 ('Programming Pearls') that fewer than 10% of professional programmers can write a correct binary search on first attempt. Off-by-one errors and integer overflow (the mid = (lo+hi)/2 overflow fix wasn't added to Java's standard library until 2006) are common pitfalls.
items.why: Algorithmic choice depends on usage pattern. Even simple algorithms have subtle correctness traps.

items.title: Recursion uses stack space
items.claim: A naive recursive Fibonacci function fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) for n=50 will:

options.text: Take roughly 2^50 (~10^15) function calls and either run for hours or exhaust the stack/timeout — naive recursion has exponential complexity even though the iteration is linear
Always crash with a syntax error

items.reveal:
Naive recursive Fibonacci recomputes the same values exponentially many times. Memoisation (caching computed values) or dynamic programming reduces it to O(n) time and O(n) or O(1) space.

Tail-call optimisation (TCO) is a compiler technique to reuse stack frames for tail-recursive calls; Scheme requires it, OCaml supports it, Python doesn't. Functional languages often rely on TCO to make recursion as cheap as iteration.
items.why: Recursion is elegant but not free. Stack depth and redundant work are common pitfalls that can be fixed without abandoning the technique.

items.title: Greedy algorithms can fail to find the optimum
items.claim: A greedy coin-change algorithm for the UK coin set {1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1, £2} always gives the optimal (fewest-coin) result. Does it work for any set of coin values?

options.text: Yes, greedy always works for coins
No — for arbitrary coin sets, greedy can fail. E.g. coins {1, 3, 4} for target 6: greedy picks 4+1+1=3 coins, but optimal is 3+3=2 coins. Dynamic programming guarantees the optimum
Greedy is always worse than dynamic programming

items.reveal_title: Greedy works for some problems, not others
items.reveal:
The UK coin set is 'canonical' — greedy works because each coin is at least twice the previous. The US set is also canonical. Some historical European sets were not.

Greedy works when the problem has the 'greedy choice' property and optimal substructure. Dynamic programming handles a broader class but needs more memory and time. Knapsack, scheduling, shortest-path — each problem has algorithms whose correctness depends on structure.
items.why: Algorithm design strategies have preconditions. Applying greedy where it doesn't fit gives wrong answers, not just slow ones.

items.title: Arrays and linked lists differ in access patterns
items.claim: For a structure where you frequently access elements by index, which is faster?

options.text: Array — O(1) random access vs linked list's O(n) traversal. Linked lists win on O(1) insertion/deletion at known nodes; arrays need O(n) for middle inserts

items.reveal:
Arrays store contiguously, so element i is at base + i*size — direct address arithmetic. Linked lists store pointers between heap-allocated nodes.

Cache effects amplify the difference: arrays are cache-friendly (linear scan loads cache lines efficiently); linked lists are cache-hostile (each node may be elsewhere in memory). For most practical workloads on modern CPUs, arrays beat linked lists even on operations linked lists 'should' win.
items.why: Big-O analysis ignores cache. Modern hardware makes the gap between theoretical and practical complexity wider — and arrays usually win.

items.title: Stacks are LIFO; queues are FIFO
items.claim: A web browser's 'back' button uses which data structure?

options.text: Stack (LIFO) — the most recent page is the first one you return to

items.reveal:
Other stack uses: function call stack (each function pushes a frame, returns pop them), expression evaluation, depth-first search, undo functionality.

Queue uses: print spoolers, BFS, message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ), CPU scheduling (round-robin), buffering in pipelines. Priority queue extends with ordering — used in Dijkstra's shortest path, OS scheduling.

The stack-based call convention is so foundational that 'stack overflow' (from recursion too deep) gave the popular Q&A site its name.
items.why: Choosing the right abstract data type clarifies the algorithm. Stack vs queue vs priority queue picks a temporal access pattern.

items.title: A BST can degenerate into a linked list
items.claim: Inserting elements 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in order into a naive binary search tree produces what?

options.text: A balanced tree with O(log n) operations
A 'right-leaning' tree that's effectively a linked list — search becomes O(n), defeating the purpose of a tree

items.reveal:
Self-balancing trees fix this: AVL trees (Adelson-Velsky & Landis, 1962), red-black trees (Bayer 1972, Guibas & Sedgewick 1978), B-trees (Bayer & McCreight 1972).

C++ std::map and Java TreeMap use red-black trees. Linux's process scheduler uses a red-black tree. Databases use B+ trees for indexes because they minimise disk I/O — a different optimisation criterion than in-memory balanced trees.
items.why: Naive implementations of textbook structures can hit worst-case behaviour easily. Production libraries use balanced variants for guaranteed bounds.

items.title: Hash tables degrade if poorly designed
items.claim: A hash table with poor hash function or no resizing can have what worst-case lookup time?

options.text: O(n) worst case if all keys hash to the same bucket; O(1) amortised expected with good hash and resizing at load factor ~0.7

items.reveal_title: Hash table performance depends on hash quality
items.reveal:
PHP, Python, Java HashMap have all had algorithmic complexity attacks where adversaries crafted inputs hashing to the same bucket, forcing O(n) lookups. Java 8 switched HashMap buckets from linked list to red-black tree above 8 entries, capping worst case at O(log n).

Cryptographic hashes (SHA-256) are slow but uniform; non-cryptographic hashes (xxHash, MurmurHash, FNV) are fast but easier to attack. SipHash (2012) was designed to be fast and collision-attack-resistant; Python adopted it for dict hashing in 3.4.
items.why: Hash tables are the workhorse of modern programming and have non-obvious failure modes. Production implementations defend against worst case.

items.title: Inheritance is often misused
items.claim: 'Favour composition over inheritance' is a widely cited OOP design guideline. What problem does it address?

options.text: Inheritance is illegal in modern languages
Deep inheritance hierarchies create tight coupling and brittle base classes; changes to a base class can break subclasses far away. Composition (holding references to other objects) is more flexible

items.reveal:
The advice traces to 'Design Patterns' (Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides, 1994 — 'Gang of Four'). Java's Date / Calendar API is a frequently-cited example of design that combined inheritance badly with mutability; it was largely replaced by java.time (JSR-310, 2014).

Go deliberately omits inheritance, providing composition and interfaces instead. Rust uses traits. Modern OOP design tends to use small interfaces and composition for code reuse, reserving inheritance for genuine subtype relationships.
items.why: Programming-language features are tools, not goals. Inheritance has its uses but is the most-overused tool in undergraduate OOP teaching.

items.title: Pure functions don't depend on or change anything outside themselves
items.claim: Which of the following is a pure function?

options.text: A function that reads from a database
A function that takes (x, y) and returns x + y, with no global state, no I/O, no mutation. Same input always produces same output
A function that writes a log file
A function whose output depends on system time

items.reveal:
Pure functions enable equational reasoning: any occurrence of f(3) can be replaced by its value with no behavioural change.

Haskell enforces purity via its type system (IO is a type that quarantines effects). Other languages (Scala, Clojure, F#) make purity easier but don't enforce it. JavaScript's reduce, map, filter encourage a functional style.

React's component model is built on the idea that UI = f(state), borrowing from functional thinking. Redux's reducers are pure functions.
items.why: Purity is a discipline that simplifies testing, parallelisation and reasoning. Even non-functional languages benefit from applying it where possible.

items.title: Race conditions appear under concurrency
items.claim: Two threads each do: count = count + 1 (where count starts at 0). What can the final value of count be?

options.text: Could be 1 or 2 depending on interleaving — the read, increment, write isn't atomic. Both threads can read 0, both write 1
The program will refuse to compile

items.reveal:
Fixes: atomic operations (AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet in Java, std::atomic in C++); locks (synchronized/mutex); message-passing concurrency (Erlang, Go channels); software transactional memory (Clojure refs).

Famous race-condition disasters: the Therac-25 radiation therapy machine (1985-87) killed three patients partly due to a race condition. The 1989 AT&T 9-hour long-distance outage was triggered by a switch software race.
items.why: Concurrency bugs are non-deterministic, hard to reproduce, and easy to write. They're a major source of production failures.

items.title: Garbage collection and ownership both manage memory
items.claim: Java and Python use garbage collection; C requires manual memory management. Rust takes a third approach. Which is it?

options.text: Rust uses garbage collection like Java
Rust uses an ownership and borrow-checking system enforced at compile time; memory is freed deterministically when the owning variable goes out of scope, with no runtime GC

items.reveal:
Rust's ownership model (one owner, borrowing rules) prevents use-after-free, double-free and data races at compile time. Graydon Hoare started Rust at Mozilla in 2006; it reached 1.0 in 2015.

Microsoft's 2019 analysis of its CVEs found ~70% were memory safety bugs in C/C++. The Linux kernel began accepting Rust modules in 2022. Android's 2023 report noted memory-safety vulnerabilities dropped from 76% (2019) to 24% (2023) as code moved to memory-safe languages.
items.why: Memory safety can be enforced at compile time, runtime (GC) or by programmer discipline. The choice trades performance, predictability and ergonomics.

items.title: RAM is volatile; storage persists
items.claim: A computer is suddenly unplugged mid-operation. What happens to data?

options.text: Data in RAM is lost (DRAM needs refresh to retain charge); data in SSD/HDD persists. This is why crash safety requires explicit flushing (fsync) to storage

items.reveal:
DRAM cells lose charge in milliseconds without refresh. SRAM (cache) holds state while powered but is volatile. SSDs (NAND flash) and HDDs are non-volatile.

Databases use write-ahead logging (WAL): changes go to log on disk before being applied to main data structures, so a crash mid-transaction can be replayed or rolled back. Filesystems (ext4, NTFS, APFS) use journaling for similar reasons. NVRAM and persistent memory (Intel Optane, discontinued 2022) blurred the boundary briefly.
items.why: The volatile/persistent distinction shapes everything from OS design to database recovery to backup strategy.

items.title: More cores don't automatically mean more speed
items.claim: Single-threaded code on a 16-core CPU runs at what speed compared to a 4-core CPU of the same generation?

options.text: Roughly the same — single-threaded code uses one core. Multi-core helps only if the workload is parallel; Amdahl's law caps speedup by the serial fraction

items.reveal:
Gene Amdahl's 1967 paper argued that if a fraction f of a program is sequential, the maximum speedup from parallelisation is 1/f. If 10% is serial, the limit is 10x even with infinite cores.

Gustafson's law (1988) softens this: for fixed time and growing problem size, you can use more cores productively. Real performance gains since ~2005 (when clock speeds plateaued) have come from cores + SIMD + GPU + algorithmic improvements, not just GHz.
items.why: Headline core counts mislead about real performance. The relevant question is what fraction of your workload can run in parallel.

items.title: ARM and x86 are different instruction set architectures
items.claim: Apple Silicon (M1, M2, M3) chips use ARM-based architecture; Intel/AMD desktop chips use x86-64. What's the main architectural difference?

options.text: ARM is a load-store RISC architecture with fixed-length instructions; x86 is a CISC architecture with variable-length instructions. ARM tends to better performance per watt; x86 has the larger software ecosystem

items.reveal:
ARM (originally Acorn RISC Machine, Cambridge, 1985) was designed for low-power embedded systems. Apple's M1 (2020) showed ARM could match or beat x86 on desktop workloads at lower power. AWS Graviton (2018) brought ARM to cloud servers.

Modern x86 chips decode CISC instructions into RISC-like micro-ops internally, so the architectural distinction is partly historical. Modern ARM (ARMv8-A and later) has grown features that blur the RISC/CISC line further.
items.why: Architecture choices that started as embedded vs desktop now overlap. Power efficiency increasingly drives the choice for both mobile and datacenter.

items.title: SSDs are dramatically faster but wear out
items.claim: SSDs (NAND flash) and HDDs (spinning disks) have different physical characteristics. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: SSDs are typically 50-100x faster than HDDs for random access, but NAND cells have finite write cycles (typically 1,000-100,000 per cell depending on technology). Wear-levelling firmware spreads writes to extend life
HDDs are always faster than SSDs

items.reveal_title: Speed at the cost of endurance
items.reveal:
HDD random access: ~5-10ms (seek + rotation). SSD random access: ~0.1ms. Sequential bandwidth: ~150MB/s HDD vs 500MB/s (SATA SSD) to 7,000MB/s+ (NVMe).

SLC NAND: ~100,000 write cycles per cell. TLC: ~3,000. QLC: ~1,000. SSD controllers use wear-levelling, over-provisioning and error correction to mask this; consumer SSDs typically last 5-10 years in normal use. HDDs fail mechanically (head crash, motor failure) rather than wearing out by writes.
items.why: Storage choice involves trade-offs of speed, capacity, cost, endurance and physical resilience. The 'right' answer depends on workload.
